title: Ezekiel 12:1–16
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel, who lives among a rebellious house, to act out exile in their sight: he prepares baggage by day, digs through a wall in the evening, and carries his baggage out in the dark with his face covered. When the people ask what he is doing, the LORD explains that the sign concerns the prince in Jerusalem and the people with him, who will go into exile. The prince will flee in the dark, be caught in the LORD’s net, and be brought to Babylon, though he will not see it. Many readers connect these details with Zedekiah’s flight and capture recorded in 2 Kings 25, Jeremiah 39, and Jeremiah 52; the accounts are best read side by side. A few will be spared to declare their abominations among the nations.

verses.text: The LORD’s word also came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel. A new message begins after the vision of chapters 8–11.

Arminian readers see God continuing to address the exiles through his prophet, offering further warning and opportunity to understand.
verses.reformedNotes:
The word introduces a sign-act performed in the exiles’ sight.

Reformed readers see God speaking through his chosen means. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s persistent communication with his people, even when they have been slow to hear.

verses.text: “Son of man, you dwell in the middle of the rebellious house, who have eyes to see, and don’t see, who have ears to hear, and don’t hear; for they are a rebellious house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Ezekiel lives among a rebellious house who have eyes but do not see and ears but do not hear. Spiritual blindness is named.

Arminian readers see willful refusal to perceive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Similar language appears in Jeremiah 5:21 and Isaiah 6:9. The phrase “rebellious house” recurs throughout Ezekiel (compare 2:5).

Reformed readers see hardened hearts. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the people’s resistance to God’s word.

verses.text: “Therefore, you son of man, prepare your baggage for moving, and move by day in their sight. You shall move from your place to another place in their sight. It may be they will consider, though they are a rebellious house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Ezekiel to prepare baggage for exile and move by day in their sight. “It may be they will consider.” A sign-act is commanded.

Arminian readers see a genuine hope that the people may respond.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase about considering suggests the sign is meant to provoke reflection.

Reformed readers see God using visible signs to teach. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s patience in warning a resistant people.

verses.text: You shall bring out your baggage by day in their sight, as baggage for moving. You shall go out yourself at evening in their sight, as when men go out into exile.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to bring out his baggage by day and go out himself in the evening, as those going into exile. The drama is staged in public view.

Arminian readers see a vivid appeal meant to catch attention where words had failed.
verses.reformedNotes:
The sign-act acts out what will happen to Jerusalem’s people and king.

Reformed readers see God’s word made visible. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the role of enacted signs in Ezekiel, which make the coming exile concrete for those who doubted it.

verses.text: Dig through the wall in their sight, and carry your baggage out that way.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to dig through the wall in their sight and carry his baggage out that way. The image is of escape by an irregular exit.

Arminian readers see an urgent picture meant to warn before the event.
verses.reformedNotes:
Digging through a wall suggests a hurried, secret flight rather than an orderly departure, as verse 12 will apply to the prince.

Reformed readers see God foretelling events through signs. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: In their sight you shall bear it on your shoulder, and carry it out in the dark. You shall cover your face, so that you don’t see the land, for I have set you for a sign to the house of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to carry the baggage on his shoulder in the dark and cover his face so as not to see the land, for the LORD has made him a sign to Israel. He becomes the message.

Arminian readers see the prophet’s life given for others’ warning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Covering the face anticipates verse 12, where the prince will not see the land.

Reformed readers see the prophet as an appointed sign. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: I did so as I was commanded. I brought out my baggage by day, as baggage for moving, and in the evening I dug through the wall with my hand. I brought it out in the dark, and bore it on my shoulder in their sight.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel does as commanded: baggage by day, digging through the wall by hand in the evening, carrying it out in the dark. The prophet obeys.

Arminian readers see faithful obedience to a strange command.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ezekiel’s exact compliance contrasts with the people’s rebellion described in verse 2.

Reformed readers see a model of obedience to God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about obedience even when the command is costly or puzzling.

verses.text: In the morning, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
In the morning the LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel. Explanation follows the sign.

Arminian readers see God interpreting the sign so that the people can understand its meaning and respond to it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The sequence of sign-act and explanation is common in Ezekiel.

Reformed readers see God both acting and explaining. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s concern that his signs be understood, so that the warning is clear and the people are left without excuse.

verses.text: “Son of man, hasn’t the house of Israel, the rebellious house, said to you, ‘What are you doing?’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks whether the rebellious house has said to Ezekiel, “What are you doing?” Curiosity provides an opening.

Arminian readers see the sign succeeding in drawing attention and opening the way for the message to be heard.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question shows that the people noticed, even if they did not yet understand.

Reformed readers see God using curiosity to deliver his word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the purpose of the sign-acts, which invite questions so that the meaning can be explained.

verses.text: “Say to them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “This burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem, and all the house of Israel among whom they are.” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to say that this burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel there. The sign is applied.

Arminian readers see the warning aimed at the king and people still in the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ezekiel uses “prince” rather than “king” here; many readers take this as a reference to Zedekiah, though the verse does not name him.

Reformed readers see God’s word addressing rulers. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the identification hedged.

verses.text: “Say, ‘I am your sign. As I have done, so will it be done to them. They will go into exile, into captivity.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to say, “I am your sign. As I have done, so will it be done to them.” They will go into exile. The meaning is plain.

Arminian readers see the sign serving as a clear warning to the people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The prophet’s actions foreshadow the coming deportation.

Reformed readers see God’s word certain to be fulfilled. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reliability of God’s warnings and the seriousness of the coming exile.

verses.text: “ ‘The prince who is among them will bear his baggage on his shoulder in the dark, and will go out. They will dig through the wall to carry things out that way. He will cover his face, because he will not see the land with his eyes.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prince will carry his baggage on his shoulder in the dark, go out through a breach in the wall, and cover his face so he will not see the land. The king’s flight is foretold.

Arminian readers see an advance warning to the king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah 39:4, 52:7, and 2 Kings 25:4 record a flight by night. Readers connect the details in different ways, and the accounts are best read side by side.

Reformed readers see God’s foreknowledge of events. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: I will also spread my net on him, and he will be taken in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon to the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it, though he will die there.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will spread his net over the prince and bring him to Babylon, “yet he will not see it, though he will die there.” The capture is foretold.

Arminian readers see judgment on a king who would not heed warnings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Many readers connect this line with the blinding of Zedekiah reported in 2 Kings 25:7, Jeremiah 39:7, and 52:11. The verse itself does not explain it.

Reformed readers see God’s word fulfilled. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: I will scatter toward every wind all who are around him to help him, and all his bands. I will draw out the sword after them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will scatter the prince’s helpers and troops to every wind and draw the sword after them. His support will be dispersed.

Arminian readers see the collapse of the help the king relied on instead of God.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 25:5 reports the king’s army scattered from him.

Reformed readers see God undoing human defenses. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the failure of military support when God has decreed judgment, and they report the event soberly.

verses.text: “ ‘They will know that I am the LORD when I disperse them among the nations and scatter them through the countries.
verses.arminianNotes:
They will know that the LORD is God when he scatters them among the nations. Knowledge comes through judgment.

Arminian readers see judgment intended to bring recognition of God and, where possible, repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
The refrain “they will know that I am the LORD” runs through Ezekiel.

Reformed readers see God making his name known. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the purpose of judgment in revealing who God is, both to Israel and among the nations.

verses.text: But I will leave a few men of them from the sword, from the famine, and from the pestilence, that they may declare all their abominations among the nations where they come. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will spare a few from sword, famine, and pestilence so they can tell of their abominations among the nations. A remnant survives as witness.

Arminian readers see mercy alongside judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
The survivors are spared so that the nations may understand the reason for the judgment; compare 14:22–23.

Reformed readers see God preserving a remnant for his purposes. Both traditions read this as shared ground about mercy within judgment.
